What if your leadership team isn’t short on feedback, but short on truth?

That’s the uncomfortable tension at the center of this week’s Polaris conversation with Petar Kralev of Mirror 360. Many leaders assume formal reviews and manager check-ins are enough to show what’s really happening. In practice, people often stay quiet when honesty feels risky, and leaders end up making decisions without the signal they need most.

One idea from the episode stands out: radical honesty only works when the system is safe, easy, and genuinely useful. If people don’t trust anonymity, the signal gets distorted. If giving input takes too long, they won’t do it. And if the insight doesn’t help employees and leaders act, it becomes just another process.

This is a thoughtful read for anyone leading teams, shaping culture, or trying to improve execution without losing the human side of work.

Global employee engagement fell to 20% in 2026, and Gallup estimates the productivity cost at $10 trillion.

That number should stop every leader in their tracks. Even more telling: a major part of the decline comes from managers themselves. When the people closest to the work are disengaged, the feedback loop breaks down fast.

That’s why Petar Kralev’s appearance on Polaris feels especially timely. In our latest article, we explore his argument that most organizations are built to document performance and reduce risk, not to reveal how work is actually experienced in real time. The result is expensive silence.

The takeaway isn’t that leaders need more surveys. They need better conditions for truth: trusted anonymity, low-friction participation, and insights people can actually use.

If you care about culture, execution, or the hidden cost of what goes unsaid, this one is worth your time.

Hot take: more feedback forms won’t fix a culture that makes honesty feel dangerous.

The usual advice is to collect more input, run another review cycle, or add another survey. But if people don’t feel safe telling the truth, more process just creates more polished silence.

That’s why Petar Kralev’s perspective on Polaris matters. The real challenge is not feedback volume. It’s feedback integrity. In our latest article, we look at why many systems are better at documentation than truth-telling, and why radical honesty depends on three things most companies still underdesign: safety, ease, and usefulness.

This is especially relevant for leaders who want better decisions, stronger teams, and fewer surprises. You can’t solve what your organization is trained to hide.

On a video call, one person kept talking. Everyone else could see the moment the room checked out. No one said it.

That memory stayed with Petar Kralev, and it helped spark the idea behind Mirror 360. In this week’s Polaris feature, we unpack how moments like that happen every day at work: problems are visible, but not speakable.

The article explores a simple but powerful idea. People are far more likely to tell the truth when feedback feels safe, takes almost no time, and gives something valuable back. That’s how honesty stops being personal risk and starts becoming a tool for growth.

For leaders, the lesson is clear: if truth only travels upward when it feels perfectly safe, then culture is not just what you say. It’s what your systems allow.
